title: Latency variance vs quantization profile — scratchpad (Sam Irani)
content:
Quick context / intent:
Trying to surface whether particular quantization profiles (and their induced noise/variance) create pathological tail behaviour under realistic arrival/concurrency patterns. Hypothesis: some quantization strategies reduce mean token latency but increase variance and p99 due to more frequent kernel fallbacks, dequant overhead, or cache eviction side-effects.

Notes about environment (baseline):
- HW: 8x A100-80GB (running same microkernel builds), test agent pinned to a single GPU for each run (no NUMA interference).
- Runtime build: local branch `latency-probes/quant` (see PR linked above). Small change: added per-kernel timing + counter for dequant ops.
- Model: open-7b-ish transformer (dense), two variants: baseline fp16 and quantized-int8-awq (layerwise grouped).
- Serving config: single-replica, continuous batching on, batch_max_tokens=4096, batch_timeout_ms=8, kv_cache enabled (TTL default), request timeout 20s.
- Arrival profiles: 1) steady Poisson at qps=25, 2) spike-saw: baseline 5 qps, burst to 200 qps for 10s every 60s, 3) steady 3 concurrency (3 inflight per connection) representing multiplexed clients.

Experiment matrix (quick):
- Quant profiles: fp16 (baseline), int8-awq (profile A), int8-symmetric (profile B), mixed-fp16/awq (drop quant on MLP).
- Sequence lengths tested: 64, 256, 1024 tokens (generation length; attention context also includes prompt ~ 128).
- Batch sizes: auto vs forced-batch-1 (to isolate batching effects).
- Run length: 10 minutes steady or 20 minutes for spike-saw.

Representative run excerpt (seq=256, arrival=spike-saw):
- fp16: p50=18ms per-token, p95=36ms, p99=87ms, mean=26ms, stddev=12ms.
- awq-int8 (profile A): p50=16ms, p95=58ms, p99=210ms, mean=35ms, stddev=48ms.
- int8-symm (profile B): p50=20ms, p95=44ms, p99=130ms, mean=30ms, stddev=28ms.
- mixed (quant MLP off): p50=17ms, p95=40ms, p99=95ms, mean=27ms, stddev=14ms.

Raw observation notes:
- AWQ reduces median/mean slightly but has frequent large tail spikes during ingress bursts. Those spikes often line up with kernel fallback logs and an increased number of dequant ops recorded by the perf counters.
- Symmetric int8 shows fewer extreme spikes than AWQ but still worse than fp16 on p99.
- Mixed profile seems a good compromise: keep quant on attention/query/key/output matmuls but execute MLP in fp16. Tail becomes similar to fp16 in most tests.
- For seq=1024 the differences amplify: awq p99 > 400ms in many runs vs fp16 p99 ~ 120ms.
- Discovered repeated small stalls (10–50ms) that correlate with cache line invalidations in the per-GPU allocator during bursts — suspect interplay between quantized kernel scratch buffers and allocator fragmentation.

Latency histogram (ASCII focus for seq=256 awq-int8 run during a burst window)
[0-10ms]: ||||||||| (8%)
[10-30ms]: ||||||||||||||| (40%)
[30-60ms]: |||||||| (20%)
[60-200ms]: ||||| (12%)
[200-1000ms]: || (2%) [these are the problematic spikes]

Quick root-cause leads and checks to run:
- Kernel fallback path: instrument the path to log (1) which kernel chosen, (2) dequant buffer allocation times, (3) whether a fallback was because of numerical range or a shape mismatch. We already added counters but need finer-grain traces (per-request).
- Allocator fragmentation: run same tests with alternative allocator (tlsf vs current) and with larger pre-allocated scratch pool. If fragmentation disappears, we know quant buffers interact badly with our scratch allocator under bursty reuse.
- KV cache eviction correlation: verify whether spikes coincide with K/V cache misses that force re-materialization. Add tagging in trace to mark cache hits/misses.
- Batch coalescing edge-case: when timeout triggers mix of long/short sequences, quant kernels might recompile or select different code paths — log kernel selection times relative to batch formation.

Quick experiments to run next (ordered):
1) Replicate AWQ spike in a smaller repro: synthetic microbenchmark that allocs + dequant per request tightly (no KV, no batching) to see if AWQ alone can produce 200ms spikes.
2) Run same workload on fp16 but throttle allocator to mimic AWQ extra mem ops to test allocator sensitivity.
3) Try pre-warming quant kernels and keep scratch pools pinned across requests (disable free) for 5m to see if spikes vanish.
4) Run mixed profile full-suite across all arrival patterns and seq lengths to quantify cost/quality tradeoff.
5) Add flamegraph collection for a tail window (p99+) to capture stacks during spikes.

Notes-to-self / open questions:
- Is AWQ kernel selecting vectorized paths that cause higher memory pressure per-thread? Need to check kernel docs w/ kernel authors (cc: Priya).
- Could numerical instability cause internal retries? Failing ranges would log but we haven't seen explicit numeric fallback errors; still worth adding in more verbose numeric checks.
- How much of the p99 delta is acceptable vs cost savings from quantization? Need to compute token-cost delta (AWS/GCP) with traffic profile.

Immediate action items (today):
- Priya: look at kernel selection logs, add per-request kernel id trace (INF-3214).
- Liam: spin allocator experiment (tlsf + prealloc) on `perf-3` testbed and share results by 2025-02-04.
- Me (Sam): build micro repro (step 1) and collect flamegraph for an AWQ spike window.

Conclusion (rough):
Quantization (especially AWQ) buys token-cost / throughput improvements on average but introduces variance and dangerous tail spikes under bursty traffic. Mixed profiles (avoid quantizing MLPs) are promising as a pragmatic default for production where p99 latency matters. Need more narrow repros to be confident — avoid shipping blanket AWQ as default until we understand allocator + kernel interactions.

Random loose thoughts (brain dump):
- Maybe expose a runtime knob: "quantization-tail-protection" that will automatically unquantize MLPs when ingress QPS crosses X or when jitter detection triggers. Could be a temporary mitigation for Dedicated customers.
- Could we maintain an LRU of pre-warmed quant kernels per-GPU to avoid repeated scratch alloc churn? This is similar to the pre-warm idea above but tied to model-version keys.

End of scratchpad. Will push a cleaned-up note to Confluence once we have reproducible microbenchmark and a small flamegraph appendix.
